title: The kitchen rota (Rule 35)
hook: everyone takes a turn serving in the kitchen, even the abbot

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ladder of humility: twelve rungs, from fear to love. Your line was humility is a ladder. Which rung did you climb, and where? Day one thousand one hundred seventeen.

Who's cooking tonight? Benedict answers that question for his whole monastery in a single chapter. The brothers, he says, are to serve one another. Nobody is let off kitchen duty. The only exceptions are the sick, and a brother busy with something more pressing for the house. Everyone else takes a week. Scholar, singer, the one who copies books, the one who hoes the beans: each in turn puts on the apron and feeds the others, and then, at the week's end, cleans up and hands the job on. A rota, in the plain old sense. A list on the wall, and your name comes round. Today's word: the kitchen rota.

Benedict gives two reasons, and neither is efficiency. First, he says, serving this way earns a greater reward. Second, it builds love. Not love as a feeling. Love as a habit of the hands, learned by carrying plates to people you didn't choose. Paul put it plainly: "by love serve one another." Now look how kind the chapter is. The weak, Benedict says, should get helpers, so nobody serves in misery. The cooks for the week get a little extra bread and drink beforehand, so they can serve without grumbling and without going hungry. He knows exactly how hungry people get while feeding others. Then the handover, on the last day of the week. The outgoing servers wash the towels. They hand back the pots and pans to the cellarer, clean and in one piece. And the servers going off and the servers coming on wash the feet of everyone in the house. Feet, after a week of serving food. It's hard not to hear Jesus here, at the last supper, a towel tied around him: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." Then, in chapel, the cook going off duty thanks God for help and comfort, and the one coming on asks for help, with a psalm verse said three times, which the King James gives as: "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD." Even the dishes start with a prayer for help. Which, if you've ever faced a sink after a big family dinner, makes sense.

Here's the practice: take a turn in the kitchen. Sit for a moment, and picture the kitchen you'll be in today, at home, at work, wherever food happens. Who usually does the serving there? Who clears up? See their face. Now choose one job that's usually theirs, and decide to take it: the dishes, the coffee, the table, the trash. No announcement. If you pray, you can say the psalm line before you start: make haste to help me. The bell holds the time.
The kitchen rota. Benedict's weekly turns of serving, so that nobody is only ever served and love becomes a habit of the hands.
Your line: everyone serves. Today, take one kitchen job that's usually someone else's. Do it without being asked, and without saying so. Day one thousand one hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: In Benedictine houses, monks and nuns take turns at serving meals and kitchen work, often by the week, and the handover is marked with prayer in chapel as the Rule describes.

match.prompt: the rota, step by step — tap the pairs.
pairs: the sick, and those on urgent work

myth: Benedict's monks hire servants to cook for them
the brothers serve one another, a week each, in turn.
the servers wash the feet of the whole house
at the week's end, those going off and those coming on wash everyone's feet.
the Rule says kitchen duty should be hard on purpose
the weak get helpers, and the cooks get extra bread so they can serve without grumbling.

fork.setup: you're the abbot drawing up the kitchen list. your best scholar asks to be let off so he can keep writing. what does the Rule say?
options: let him off. his work matters more.
only the sick, or someone on more urgent business, is excused.
let him pay someone else to take his week.
fork.reveal: nobody is let off kitchen service except for sickness, or work of greater need for the house. serving builds love.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rota is just a chore chart.
what it means: in Benedict's Rule, the turns of serving are how love becomes a habit of the hands.
what a scholar hears: the week ends with foot-washing, echoing John 13, and begins with Psalm 70, make haste to help me.

notes: The index hook says 'even the abbot'. Rule 35 says no one is excused except for sickness or more useful business; it does not name the abbot, and Rule 56 gives the abbot a separate table with guests. The script does not claim the abbot cooks. A Keeper may want the index hook revised.

Rule 35 paraphrased: greater reward and charity; helpers for the weak; servers receive drink and bread an hour before the meal so they serve without murmuring; Saturday cleaning, towels, feet; utensils returned clean and whole to the cellarer; the Sunday verses in the oratory. The outgoing verse (Daniel 3:52 / Psalm 86:17 in the Rule) is described, not quoted.
The incoming server's verse in the Rule is the Vulgate's Psalm 69:2 ('Deus in adiutorium meum intende...'); quoted here from KJV Psalm 70:1, whose wording differs. Confirm this is acceptable.
No word count is claimed for Galatians 5:13.
'The foot-washing echoes John 13' is an interpretive link; the Rule itself does not cite John 13 in chapter 35. The script says 'it's hard not to hear Jesus here' rather than claiming the source.
The hook's 'it can start an argument in any home' is a light joke, not a claim.

Editor pass: Rule 35 has both the outgoing and incoming servers wash everyone's feet, so the teach, match and myth were corrected; the Psalm 70:1 line is now framed as the King James wording of the verse; cut the 'any home' sweep and the empty 'it's beautiful'.

Audit pass: the hook's 'who does the dishes... start an argument' repeated day 1111's family-argument-over-dishes opening, so it now opens on who's cooking; fixed a garbled lowercase sentence start; John 13:4–5 says Jesus girded himself with a towel, not that he knelt, so 'kneeling' was replaced.
